findings.issue: “Structure decides the strongest force” and the unqualified table turn a useful first-pass guide into a universal rule. In particular, a polar molecule without H bonded to N/O/F does not invariably have dipole-dipole as its dominant net interaction; molecular size and polarizability also matter.
findings.evidence: The source's justification step explicitly includes size/polarizability and ionic charge, while core_idea and the CED state that London dispersion is often the strongest net IMF between large molecules. The reference comparison of polar and nonpolar molecules is limited to molecules of comparable size. The table needs a comparable-size/simple-case qualifier or an explicit size/polarizability exception.

findings.issue: “This ranking decides solid type and properties … and which substances mix” is deterministic and overstates what IMF ranking can predict. IMF ranking alone does not determine whether a solid is ionic, covalent-network, molecular, or metallic, and mixing is not guaranteed by an IMF-strength ranking.
findings.evidence: CED 3.2 distinguishes solid classes by their particles and bonding. CED 3.10 says substances with similar IMFs tend to be miscible/soluble; it does not say an IMF ranking decides mixing. The source describes the ranking as a mechanism behind classification and solubility/miscibility prediction, so “helps explain/predict,” together with IMF similarity and “tend to,” would preserve the intended meaning.
